summary: An island country in the western Indian Ocean made up of 115 islands, known for its beaches and coral reefs; it is the least populous country in Africa and became independent from Britain in 1976.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Seychelles was formally colonized by the French only in 1770, and both the French settlers and the African and Malagasy slaves brought there were influenced by Catholicism. Britain gained control in 1814, but the local French culture and Catholic tradition did not change; from the mid-19th century Capuchin Catholic missionaries preached systematically, and Africans rescued from slave ships by the Royal Navy and settled here were also mostly baptized as Catholics. Catholicism therefore remains the overwhelmingly dominant religion.

ranking.name: Other Christianity (Pentecostal, Seventh-day Adventist, etc.)
ranking.description: Newer denominations such as the Pentecostal and Seventh-day Adventist churches arrived mainly in the late 20th century, and after multiparty democracy was restored in 1993 religious activity became freer still. These churches attract some former Catholics with fervent worship, community care and radio evangelism, and their believers are mostly concentrated in the towns of Mahé.

ranking.name: Anglicanism
ranking.description: The Anglican Church was introduced during British colonial rule (1814–1976), when British missionaries set up churches and schools in the 19th century. However, because the Catholic tradition had already been established in the French period, the Anglican Church has always attracted only a minority of inhabitants, mainly British officials, some Creoles and families with an English-language educational background.

ranking.name: Hinduism
ranking.description: Hindus are mainly Tamils, and their descendants, who came from southern India to trade or work from the late 19th century. They built Hindu temples in the capital, Victoria, and hold festivals such as Thaipusam; these are the core of the cultural identity of the Indian community in Seychelles, but the numbers are very small.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam was brought mainly by Muslim traders from Gujarat in India and elsewhere and by East African immigrants, who engaged in retail and trade in Victoria. A mosque was built in Victoria in the 1980s, but the Muslim community has always been small.

religion.background: The Seychelles islands were uninhabited before the 18th century; French colonization in 1770 brought Catholicism, and African and Malagasy slaves were also forced to be baptized. Britain took over in 1814 and brought Anglicanism, but Catholicism remained the mainstream. Indian and Chinese immigrants from the late 19th century brought Hinduism, Islam and Buddhism. After independence in 1976 the constitution guaranteed religious freedom, and the Catholic Church still has great influence in education and social life.

language.official: The official languages are Seychellois Creole, English and French.

ranking.name: Seychellois Creole
ranking.description: Seychellois Creole is a French-based creole that developed between French settlers and African and Malagasy slaves after French colonization in 1770. For a long time it was regarded as an informal spoken language; the René government, which came to power in the 1977 coup, raised it to a national symbol, and in 1981 it officially became an official language and was used for teaching in primary schools. Today almost all Seychellois speak Creole at home.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: The status of English comes from British colonial rule of 1814–1976, and after independence it remains the main language of government administration, law and education from secondary school up. Because of the needs of tourism and international trade, English ability is important in society, but only a minority have English as a mother tongue.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: French was the language of the earliest colonists in the 18th century, and even through more than a hundred years of British rule the Catholic Church and upper-class families long continued to use French, so French culture has persisted in Seychelles. Today French is one of the official languages and is still used in the church, the media and some education, but very few people have it as a mother tongue.

language.history: Seychellois Creole formed in the 18th century during French colonial times, based on French vocabulary and blending elements of Bantu and Malagasy languages. After Britain took over in 1814 English became the language of administration, but French continued in circulation in the church and in the upper levels of society. After independence in 1976 the government promoted the standardization of Creole, and in 1981 it became an official language and entered the schools. Today the three official languages coexist, and Creole is the common mother tongue of the nation.

ranking.name: Fish curry
ranking.description: Tuna or other sea fish stewed with coconut milk, turmeric, garlic, ginger and curry spices and eaten with white rice, rich and mildly spicy.
ranking.history: The curry method came from Indian traders and laborers who arrived in Seychelles in the late 19th century and, combined with French Creole cooking, formed an island flavor blended with coconut milk. The waters around Seychelles are rich in fish, fishing has long been an important livelihood, and the capital, Victoria, also has a large tuna cannery. Fish curry with white rice is almost the everyday meal of every household and also a signature dish at festivals such as the Creole Festival.

ranking.name: Ladob (coconut milk and banana dessert)
ranking.description: A sweet soup of ripe cooking bananas or breadfruit cooked in coconut milk with sugar, nutmeg and vanilla; there is also a savory version with salted fish.
ranking.history: The name "ladob" derives from the French "daube" (stew), reflecting the culinary influence of the French colonial period. The French grew spice crops such as vanilla, nutmeg and cinnamon in Seychelles, and these spices thus entered everyday desserts. It is often made at family gatherings, religious holidays and the Creole Festival and is the most representative dessert of Seychelles.

ranking.name: Satini reken (shark chutney)
ranking.description: Small shark meat is cooked and mashed and mixed with lime juice, onion, turmeric and the local sour fruit bilimbi to make a sour and spicy shark relish.
ranking.history: "Satini" comes from the Hindi "chutney" (a sour and spicy relish), brought to Seychelles through Indian Ocean trade and Indian immigrants and combined with the island's abundant catch. Shark is one of the fish traditionally caught by Seychellois fishermen, and mashing it into a relish both preserves it and makes it convenient to eat with rice. It is the dish with the most island character among Creole home cooking and often appears on festival tables.

ranking.name: Breadfruit
ranking.description: Breadfruit is a large starchy fruit that can be roasted, fried, boiled or made into chips, with a creamy texture, often taking the place of rice as a staple or made into desserts.
ranking.history: Breadfruit is native to the Pacific islands and was introduced to the Indian Ocean islands by French colonists in the late 18th century; it grows extremely well in Seychelles' hot, humid climate and quickly became an important food crop. In the days when rice had to be imported, breadfruit was the staple of many households. A local saying goes, "Whoever has eaten breadfruit will surely return to Seychelles," and it has thus become one of the symbols of Seychelles.

ranking.name: Grilled fish
ranking.description: Whole inshore fish such as red snapper rubbed with a marinade of garlic, ginger, chili and lime and grilled over charcoal, with a charred, fragrant skin and tender, juicy flesh.
ranking.history: The Seychelles islands are surrounded by coral reefs, and before the rise of tourism, fishing and the growing of copra and spices were the inhabitants' main livelihoods. After the international airport opened in 1971 tourism developed rapidly, and grilled sea fish also became the signature dish of beach restaurants. Locals often grill fish at weekend family gatherings and beach picnics, served with Creole chili sauce and rice, the most everyday and most island-flavored dish.
